1:
Which five brethren were chosen, and why, turns on a single obscure phrase, and Clarke lays out six answers to it. Literally the words say that from the end or extremity of his brethren he took five men, which has been understood to mean five at random; or five of the meanest-looking, lest Pharaoh detain the sightlier for his own service and their religion be corrupted; or five of the best made, to impress the king with the family just brought into Egypt; or five of the youngest; or five of the eldest; or, on a rabbi's authority, some from each end. He allows that it may also mean simply some out of the whole. Gill runs through the same list and concludes that he made no choice at all but took some that offered next. Ellicott counts the number instead, noting that five recurs in this narrative and may have had special importance among the Egyptians, as seven had among the Jews.

The interview itself is read as a lesson in station. Henry marks the respect Joseph showed as a subject, since though he was the favourite and prime minister, and had the king's own orders to send for his father, he would not suffer him to settle until he had given notice of it; and the respect he showed as a brother, since though he was a great man and they comparatively mean, he owned them. From this he draws the rule that the rich and great should not despise their poor relations, asking whether, because a branch is a lower branch, it is therefore not of the tree; and he turns the presentation into a figure, that our Lord, like Joseph, is not ashamed to call us brethren and presents them in the court of heaven though in themselves unworthy. On the question about their occupation, Wesley takes Pharaoh's assumption for the doctrine: all that have a place in the world should have an employment in it according to their capacity, so that those who need not work for their bread must yet have something to do to keep them from idleness. Gill supposes it a usual question to those coming to settle, that the king might have no idle vagrants; Ellicott explains why they were told to add that their fathers were shepherds too, since occupations were hereditary among the Egyptians and Pharaoh would conclude no change of life was possible for them.

What they asked for is smaller than what was offered, and Calvin makes that the point. Pharaoh offers a perpetual home and they rather wish to depart, and it is to be ascribed to the favour of God that he was not offended, since nothing is more indignantly borne by kings than that their favours should be rejected. He rejects the plausible explanation that this was modesty, since it would have been proud to ask for the rights of citizens: the suggestion is fallacious, for in asking to be admitted as guests and strangers they took timely precaution that Pharaoh should not hold them in the chains of servitude. Wesley and Gill read it the same way, that they came to sojourn and not to settle for ever, keeping in mind that Canaan was their inheritance. Ellicott adds why Goshen could still keep flocks in a famine, since the river, though it did not overflow, probably lost itself in delta swamps which produced much marsh grass. Clarke, on the offer to make them rulers over the king's cattle, argues that the word means possessions of any kind, and asks whether Pharaoh would set the brethren of his prime minister to the meanest offices in the land; he takes the king to mean that they should oversee his domestic concerns while Joseph superintended those of the state.
7:
The blessing Jacob gives is weighed first, and not all will let it be a greeting. Clarke takes it for a salutation, peace be unto thee or the like. Calvin denies that this is all: the term does not mean a common and profane salutation but the pious prayer of a servant of God, since the children of this world salute kings for the sake of honour and by no means raise their thoughts to God, whereas Jacob adjoins to civil reverence that affection which commends the king's safety to God; and he draws the duty from it, that if captives were commanded to pray for the peace of the city of their exile, because their own peace was involved in it, Jacob owed as much to a king so humane, and we are commanded to pray for whatever rulers we have. Ellicott explains why the interview was more solemn than that of the brethren, whom Pharaoh had received as the kinsmen of his vizier: to an Egyptian a hundred and twenty was the utmost limit of longevity, and Jacob was a hundred and thirty, so the king probably bowed before him as a saintly personage and twice received a formal benediction rather than the usual prayer for the royal life.

Whether pilgrimage is the right word for the answer divides two of them exactly. Clarke traces the English word through the French to a Latin term for a stranger, one abroad and not at home, and defines a pilgrim as a person who took a journey on some religious account, submitting to many hardships; a more appropriate term, he says, could not be conceived for the life of Jacob, since apart from the journey to Mesopotamia the principal part of his travels were pilgrimages undertaken in the course of God's providence. Ellicott denies it flatly: the idea of a pilgrimage is a modern one, and Jacob was no traveller bound by religious motives to some distant shrine but a sojourner, because Canaan was not the native land of his race. Gill and Wesley keep the word and make it a doctrine, that every good man's life is a pilgrimage since he is not at home in his own country but seeking a better; and Gill adds that Jacob's was one literally, running through Canaan, Padanaram, Succoth, Shechem, Hebron and now Egypt, and cites a heathen writer who put his age at the descent at the same figure.

Whether the answer is a complaint is the harder question. Calvin raises it against Jacob and then answers for him: he might seem to complain of the shortness of life, and the complaint would be unworthy of him, for why should a century and a third not suffice? But if the words are rightly weighed he is expressing gratitude, extolling the vigour divinely afforded to his fathers rather than deploring his own decrepitude, so that the comparison was made only to ascribe glory to God; and in naming the days evil he shows he was consumed not by years but by labours, his senses having yet been vigorous had his strength not been exhausted by continual labour and grievous suffering. Nothing, Calvin concludes, was less in the holy man's mind than to expostulate with God. Ellicott takes evil as plain biography and lists what made it so: the deceiving of his father, the toil and injustice at Haran, a pursuit behind and a menacing brother in front, the long illness at Succoth, his daughter's dishonour and his sons' fierce conduct, the loss of Rachel within sight of home, and ten years of mourning for Joseph. Henry and Wesley turn the reckoning by days into the lesson: even by days life is soon reckoned, and we are not sure of it for a day; the hoary head is only a crown of glory when found in the way of righteousness.
13:
The famine is read first as a judgment on the fertile. Calvin calls it a memorable judgment of God that the most fertile regions, accustomed to supply distant nations, were reduced almost to nothing, and draws the moral for those who cultivate rich lands: not to trust their abundance, but to acknowledge that provision does not so much spring from the earth as flow down from heaven by the secret blessing of God, since no luxuriance is so great that it is not soon exchanged for barrenness when God sprinkles it with salt instead of rain. Henry adds a second point: if the usual favours of providence are suspended but for a while we all perish, and our wealth would not keep us from starving if the rain of heaven were withheld two or three years; but see also how much we smart by our own improvidence, for if the Egyptians had done for themselves in the seven years of plenty as Joseph did for Pharaoh they had not now been in these straits. He observes too that Joseph, who might have gone to live with his father in Goshen, kept as closely as ever to his office, since even natural affection must give way to necessary business.

Whether the policy was just is the question, and the three who raise it defend it, though Calvin states the charge first. It was a miserable spectacle, he says, one which might have softened hearts of iron, to see rich farmers who had stored provision for others now begging food; so Joseph might be deemed cruel in not giving bread freely to the exhausted but robbing them of their cattle. But seeing that Joseph is transacting the business of another, he dare not charge his strictness with cruelty. Had he extorted corn by force during the fruitful years he would now have acted tyrannically; but the people had been free to store what they sold to the king, and now pay the just penalty of their negligence. Besides, since it was lawful to sell corn it was lawful to exchange it for cattle, the corn belonging to the king; and if the objection is that the poor should be helped, then were that rule to prevail the greater part of sales would be unlawful, since no one freely parts with what he possesses. He adds that Joseph was not dealing with his own property but had been appointed over the corn to gain for the king, and that since we stand or fall by God's judgment alone it is not for us to condemn what his law has left undecided.

Clarke and Ellicott defend the same measure on economic grounds. Clarke calls the taking of the cattle the wisest measure that could have been adopted for the preservation of both people and beasts, since the people had no grain and must else have divided their own portion with the cattle, which they wished to keep for tillage; bought by Joseph, the beasts were maintained at the royal expense and very likely returned at the end of the famine, for how else could the ground be cultivated? For this part of his conduct, he says, Joseph deserves high praise and no censure. Ellicott calls it a merciful arrangement by which the owners were delivered from a burden while some cattle were saved against the time they would be needed, and finds in the difficulty of keeping so many beasts in a dearth the reason why the ablest of Joseph's brethren had been wanted over the royal herds. On the second year Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin and Gill agree that it is not the second of the famine but the year after the cattle were given up; and Calvin adds what the people's plea shows, that they had become wise too late, neglecting the admonition of God when they ought to have provided.
20:
Joseph has been accused of reducing a free people to slavery, and all three answer the charge on different ground. Ellicott concedes that he vastly increased the royal power, and argues that this was to the people's advantage, since they had lived in vassalage to a multitude of petty sovereigns, and to their wives and priests besides; he adds that the Greek historians confirm that all the land belonged to the crown, as it still does in India and Burmah. Calvin answers from the conduct of the transaction: no wiles, no force and no threats had reduced the Egyptians to this necessity, and Joseph extorted nothing but treated with them at their own request. He will not rest there, conceding that a man who exploits necessity is not excused merely because the sufferer offered the terms; he argues that Joseph acted with equity in the terms themselves, conceding personal liberty, covenanting only for the fields, and restoring not only the lands but the implements he had bought. Then he turns the case on his readers: let those too intent on wealth beware of employing Joseph's example as a pretext, since all contracts not formed by the rule of charity are vicious in God's sight.

Clarke reconstructs the constitution. Before Joseph, he says, Egypt was a limited monarchy: the king had his estates, the priests their lands, the people their patrimony independent of both, so Pharaoh had no power to levy taxes until he had bought the right each man had in his possessions. He cites the historian's threefold division, one part to the priests for the sacrifices, a second to the king for his court and wars, so that there were no taxes, and the rest to the subjects, who served as a standing militia. This, he says, was a constitution something like the British, the government mixed and the monarchy properly limited, until Joseph by buying the land made the king in some sort despotic; though no improper use appears to have been made of it. Calvin thinks the fifth part light, since kings elsewhere demanded tithes and doubled them in war; and he holds that a fifth of the produce rather than of the land was chosen to induce the Egyptians to cultivate with more alacrity, convinced they were treated with clemency. He quotes an emperor otherwise reckoned a tyrant, that it is a shepherd's part to shear the flock and not to tear off the skin, and complains that in his own day kings think they do not rule freely unless they not only flay their subjects but devour them.

The exemption of the priests interests all three differently. Clarke takes it as constitutional history, their portion being assigned by Pharaoh, and calls this the earliest account we have of an established religion supported by the state. Ellicott confirms it from the historians, who report a daily allowance of cooked food to the priests and name the king, the priests and the warriors as the only landholders, and notes that the text ascribes it to the king, not to Joseph. Calvin makes it evidence about human nature, that a heathen king so attended to divine worship as to support the priests gratuitously, which shows that a sentiment of piety is implanted in men and cannot be wholly effaced; he calls the object of it foolish superstition and the design in itself worthy of commendation, and turns it against Christian princes who neglect ministers they know to be approved by God, when this king nourished his own to his destruction. He then asks whether Joseph could lawfully feed such priests, and answers that he dare not absolutely condemn the act, nor deny that he may have erred in not resisting the superstition more boldly, since no law required him to destroy them by hunger and he could no more deny them the king's corn than the nobles.
27:
Why Jacob should care so much where his body lay is the question the oath forces, and Calvin gives the fullest answer. He infers from it not only the old man's anxiety but his invincible magnanimity, since none of the wealth of Egypt could prevent him from sighing after a land in which he had passed a laborious life; and his faith appeared more excellent still in this, that by commanding his body to be carried back he encouraged his sons to hope for deliverance, so that being dead he animated the living as with the sound of a trumpet. For to what purpose was such care about a sepulchre, except that the promise of God might be confirmed to his posterity? Calvin adds a political reason the others miss: this choice of burial would not gratify the Egyptians, looking like a reproach on their kingdom, as though the stranger could find no fit place in that splendid country; so Jacob bound Joseph by an oath that he might more freely dare to ask the favour, and Joseph afterwards used that plea to avoid giving offence. He notes why the office fell on Joseph rather than the brothers, who as strangers had neither favour nor authority, and that Joseph most needed guarding lest, ensnared by Egypt, he should forsake his own kindred.

The others give warmer and simpler reasons. Ellicott seeks no remote reason, since Jacob's nature was loving and strongly domestic, and at the cave his nearest relatives lay — the grandfather he had known as a boy, his father and mother, and Leah, who had at last won his affections — so he wished to lie among his own; against which he sets the grief that Rachel was buried apart. Wesley and Gill make it faith rather than affection: he would be buried there not because it was the land of his nativity but because it was the land of promise, which he desired thus to keep possession of until his posterity were masters of it, and a type of that better country he expected. Gill adds that the choice would draw his sons' minds off from continuing in Egypt. Calvin, on lying with his fathers, observes that the word sleep, when put for dying, refers to the body and not the soul, for what did it concern him to be buried with them except to testify that he was joined to them after death by a bond death could not extinguish?

The last clause is a textual crux, and the commentators divide over a single unpointed word. Ellicott explains that the Hebrew without vowels may mean either bed or staff, that the Greek version and the epistle following it read the top of his staff, and that the vowel points were added later and are not of final authority; he still prefers the received rendering, since it was scarcely worth mentioning that Jacob bowed leaning on a staff, whereas the patriarch leaning back upon his bed, content in his son's promise, is a picture full of pathos. Clarke gives both and lets the reader choose, offering the plain sense that the exhausted old man, having sat up to take the oath, reclined again upon his bed; he reports that some have supposed a carved image on the staff's head, or that Jacob bowed to Joseph's sceptre and so fulfilled the dreams, and prefers, on the other reading, that leaning on his staff he bowed in adoration to God. Calvin takes the bed, holding that Jacob, unable to rise, composed himself in the attitude of prayer, and explains the Greek rendering as an error of similar words which the apostle followed as commonly used; an editor's note inside the same block answers him flatly, that this reasoning is in every respect unsatisfactory and founded on a misquotation, the whole difference lying in the disputed Masoretic points.
